title: American Airlines planes made contact while taxiing for takeoff at Washington, DC, airport
summary: Runway wing collision at Reagan National involving two American Airlines jets adds to FAA scrutiny two weeks after recent nationwide flight grounding.
content: American Airlines aircraft make contact on runway. Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images Two American Airlines planes clipped wings at Reagan National while taxiing. No injuries were reported, but both planes returned, and debris had to be cleared from the tarmac. The incident follows a recent FAA system outage and a deadly crash near the same airport. Two planes made contact on the runway at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Friday evening. American Airlines Flight 638, bound for Dallas, clipped the wing of American Airlines Flight 2152, headed for Chicago, while taxiing. "Both planes returned to gates and were checked by Airports Authority Fire and Rescue personnel," the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority said in a statement shared with Business Insider. "No injuries were reported and there was no disruption to other flights." While the collision did not affect other flights, those two planes were taken back to the gate. A passenger on the flight going to Chicago told BBC that the "aircraft shook quite violently," and he heard gasps in the cabin. Audio from the radio traffic indicates part of a plane's wing was broken off, and there was debris on the tarmac from the incident. A statement from American Airlines said the two aircraft were removed from service for inspection. Two American Airlines flights set to take off for Dallas and Chicago clipped their wings at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA) on Friday, according to federal aviation officials. No injuries were reported. https://t.co/4ucOg4l53A — 7News DC (@7NewsDC) November 28, 2026 "We apologize to our customers for the inconvenience and are working to get them on their way as soon as possible," the statement sent to Business Insider said. This incident comes two weeks after a day of a nationwide grounding of all flights by the Federal Aviation Administration. An issue with air traffic control systems led to about 12,500 flights being canceled. Nearly two years ago, an American Airlines flight and a Black Hawk helicopter collided in Washington, DC, killing 67 people. Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, in Arlington, Virginia, just outside Washington, DC, is about 3 miles from the White House and has one of the busiest runways in the country . The cause of the recent FAA trouble has yet to be confirmed, but federal officials have pointed to AI as a potential cause for the outages. The reason for the wing clipping is unknown at the moment, but the FAA said in a statement that it will investigate the situation. Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Meet Lululemon founder Chip Wilson, who continues to spark controversy even away from the company
summary: Chip Wilson, who founded Lululemon in 1997, sparked fresh controversy after telling a leadership forum that Canadian women aren't having enough kids.
content: Lululemon founder Chip Wilson in 2017. Jim Bennett/Getty Images Chip Wilson founded Lululemon Athletica Inc. in 1997 after selling his first apparel company. During his tenure, Wilson became known for his inappropriate remarks and mishandling of scandals. He's been vocal about his negative views of Lululemon's leadership and continues to draw attention. Lululemon's billionaire founder, Chip Wilson, hasn't been at the helm in over a decade, but still continues to draw controversy to the brand. Wilson, an American-born Canadian, started Lululemon in the 90s and has been at the forefront of the athleisure movement , which is estimated to reach $623 billion by 2030, according to a November 2025 report . Wilson doesn't run the company — and hasn't in years — but isn't shy about voicing his opinions on how the brand should be run. Wilson has previously critiqued the company and even attempted to put new leadership in place . But outside the controversy within the company, Wilson has brought attention to himself in other ways. While speaking at a leadership conference in November, Wilson made comments to the audience suggesting women in Canada are having too few children, potentially leading to men seeking wives outside the country. He's still linked to Lululemon as the largest individual shareholder, and is in the top 50 richest Canadians, according to Canadian magazine Maclean's . He spends part of his fortune on philanthropy and researching a cure for the rare muscular disease called facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy, which he was diagnosed with at 32 years old. Here's everything we know about Wilson's life and career as the founder and former CEO of Lululemon. Dennis “Chip” Wilson was born in California and raised in Canada. Chip Wilson, Lululemon founder. Reuters Wilson lived in California up until the age of five when his family moved to Calgary. He relocated to Edmonton for university in 1973 before moving back to the US for work two years later, according to his website. He worked on an oil pipeline and as an economist before venturing into entrepreneurship. Michael Buckner/Getty He lived in Alaska and worked on an oil pipeline in 1975. During this time, Wilson said he read the top 100 books of all time. "By the age of 19, I might have been the wealthiest, most traveled and best-read boy in the world," Wilson wrote on his website. He went on to become an economist after receiving his degree in economics from the University of Calgary in 1979. He attributes his first entrepreneurial success to a mistake. Steve Russell/Getty His entrepreneurial streak began in 1979 with Westbeach Surf Company. He started making shorts inspired by those he saw on a trip to California in 1979, Wilson writes in his book, "The Story of Lululemon." "The mistake that led to my success was an inability to sell my long, baggy, wild-patterned shorts to wholesalers. Consequently, I was forced to open my own store," he writes on his website. He opened his own stores and owned the manufacturing — a move that he said tripled profits, he writes Over the years, his company evolved to serve different types of athletic lifestyles, like skateboarding and snowboarding. In 1997, Wilson sold Westbeach. He was diagnosed with FSHD2 in 1987 at the age of 32. Athletes during the swim portion of the Ironman challenge in Lisbon, Portgual. Octavio Passos/Getty Images Wilson led an active lifestyle growing up. He played football, wrestled in university, and completed an Ironman triathlon in 1983, according to his website. Four years later, he was diagnosed with the rare, slow-atrophying muscular dystrophy. Ten years later, he founded the athleisure brand Lululemon. UCG/Getty The first Lululemon store opened in 2000 in Vancouver, Forbes reported. Wilson is often credited with creating and normalizing athleisure for everyday wear rather than just for workouts. Wilson once said he named the company Lululemon because he believed Japanese people couldn't pronounce the letter L. "It's funny to watch them try and say it," Wilson told Canada's The Tyee in 2005. He has also said that brand names with the letter L in them are considered more authentic to Japanese consumers. His now-wife, Summer Wilson, started as the founding lead designer for the brand, according to her website. He married Summer Wilson in 2002 and has five sons. Robert Cianflone/Getty Images Wilson and Summer wed in 2002, according to his site. He had two sons from a previous marriage, and he and Summer eventually welcomed three more. The couple lives in Vancouver, where Wilson has lived permanently since 1986, per his website. Wilson stepped down as CEO of Lululemon in 2005. Brad Barket/Getty Wilson sold 48% of his stake in Lululemon to two private equity firms and stepped down as CEO. His successor as CEO was former Starbucks executive Christine Day. The company went public in 2007. He served as the company’s chief innovation and branding officer for about 4 years before he was forced to resign. Foot traffic at Lululemon stores increased 11% in February, according to a new report. Budrul Chukrut/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty Images In January 2012, Lululemon announced that Wilson would step down from his role as chief innovation and branding officer. His vision for the brand's direction was a source of friction between him and former CEO Day. Following his resignation, Wilson began a sabbatical in Australia for over a year before Lululemon called him back to help handle a crisis, according to a 2015 press release. Wilson has made some outrageous remarks about women, child labor, and more over the years. Penske Media/Getty Women, children, and minorities have been the subject of Wilson's most offensive takes over the years. Most of which he's had to later clarify or apologize for. The lululemon founder once blamed birth control for higher divorce rates since "Men did not know how to relate to the new female." Wilson has also spoken in favor of children working in factories to earn money and avoid poverty. "The single easiest way to spread wealth around the world is to have poor countries pull themselves out of poverty," Wilson told The Tyee . His comments about women’s bodies preceded Wilson's official departure from Lululemon. Justin Sullivan/Getty Customers began complaining about their pants pilling in 2013, months after Lululemon had to recall 17% of its pants for being too sheer. Wilson — the chairman of the board at that time — responded to the criticism during an interview with Bloomberg TV by saying their own bodies might be to blame rather than Lululemon. "Frankly some women's bodies just don't actually work for it," Wilson told Bloomberg. "They don't work for some women's bodies...it's really about the rubbing through the thighs, how much pressure is there over a period of time, how much they use it." He eventually apologized for his remarks in a YouTube video posted to Lululemon's Facebook page after his comments caused public outrage. Wilson stepped down as chairman of the board in 2013. Jim Bennett/Getty Amid tension with Day and a year of scandals for Lululemon, Wilson stepped down from his role as chairman of the board in 2013. In his book, titled "Little Black Stretchy Pants," Wilson said he made Day cry during a 2013 meeting when he called her a terrible CEO and questioned her vision for Lululemon. Wilson wrote that he suspected her reaction was fake, and Day announced her resignation one day later. On his website, Wilson said he had his own reason for leaving the company. "I lost control of the culture and product development," Wilson wrote. "At odds with a board of directors who did not want to invest in the future, I departed in 2013." In 2014, Wilson sold half of his stake in Lululemon. Zhang Peng/Getty In the deal, Wilson sold half of his shares in the company to investment firm Advent International for $845 million, Inc. reported . Today, Wilson owns an approximate 8% stake in Lululemon, according to Bloomberg . Wilson owns about 1% of Anta Sports, which is known as the Nike of China. The logo of Anta Sports is seen on its product during a news conference in Hong Kong Thomson Reuters In 2019, Wilson invested $100 million in the Chinese activewear company for a 0.6% stake, Forbes reported . Anta owns a majority stake in Amer Sports, a conglomerate of brands which includes Arc'teryx and Wilson Sports. Wilson said in an interview that he owns a 20% stake in Amer. Wilson has a $5.1 billion net worth. Gary Hershorn/Getty Wilson's approximately 8% stake in Lululemon is the largest individual stake in the company, according to Forbes , which lists his net worth at $5.1 billion. Lululemon reported $11.1 billion in revenue in 2025. He owns the most expensive home in Vancouver. Ron Watts/Getty Images His waterfront mansion was valued at $73.4 million CAD (about $51.4 million) in 2026 and has seven bedrooms and nine bathrooms, according to CBC . The property, which was constructed in 2008, has a pool and tennis court. In 2011, Wilson and his wife launched a real estate company. Rachel Murray/Getty Low Tide Properties invests in, develops, and operates commercial and residential buildings in Vancouver, with a focus on building lab and hospital spaces. It also owns multi-family properties in Seattle. Wilson told Real Estate Magazine that he started the company with a goal to invest 65% of his family's wealth into real estate in three cities by 2030. The couple also started a design school. Chip Wilson, Summer Wilson, and JJ Wilson attend the Kit and Ace launch party. Paul Marotta/Getty In 2018, the Wilsons established the Wilson School of Design at Kwantlen Polytechnic University in Richmond, British Columbia. They donated $12 million towards the program and a $36 million new facility on the school's campus. Wilson has charitable organizations for education and land conservation. Chip and Summer Wilson attend a Imagine1Day dinner event Rachel Murray/Getty He has allocated some of his wealth toward his charities Imagine1Day, which funds schooling for children in Ethiopia, and the Wilson 5 Foundation, which supports land conservation and public art installations in British Columbia. He allocated $100 million into his venture to cure FSHD. YouTube/TEDx Talks Wilson's rare muscular disease affects an estimated 900,000 people globally. Wilson has an even less common form known as FSHD2, which affects just 5% of those with the disease, Business Insider reported. In 2022, Wilson created his philanthropic venture Solve FSHD and pledged $100 million into finding a cure for FSHD. Wilson has unusual views on aging and has tried anti-aging treatments. Chip Wilson On his website, Wilson wrote, "I have a great fascination for the subject of longevity as I see aging as a disease." In his quest to cure FSHD, he has experimented with longevity and wellness treatments popular among wealthy entrepreneurs trying to prevent aging. Some of his methods include hormone therapy, electroacupuncture, and daily doses of the immunosuppressive drug rapamycin, according to Bloomberg . Since stepping down, he's been critical of Lululemon's business strategies. credit should read CFOTO/Future Publishing via Getty Images Wilson told Forbes in an interview published in January 2024 that he doesn't agree with the "whole diversity and inclusion thing" that Lululemon has embraced. "They're trying to become like the Gap, everything to everybody. And I think the definition of a brand is that you're not everything to everybody," Wilson said. "You've got to be clear that you don't want certain customers coming in," he added. Wilson has had some choice words for Lululemon's leadership over the years as the brand loses ground to brands like Alo Yoga and Vuori. In October 2025, he compared the mistakes that the brand has made to a plane crash. He also doesn't appear to be a fan of CEO Calvin McDonald , who is set to exit the company in 2026. He blamed the brand's "loss of cool" on McDonald and his team for losing its innovative edge, The Wall Street Journal reported . In December 2025, he launched a proxy fight in an effort to shake up Lululemon's board Jim Bennett/Getty Images Although Wilson hasn't held a management position at Lululemon in over a decade, he's still voicing his strong opinions on how the company should be run. After Lululemon named CFO Meghan Frank and chief commercial officer André Maestrini as co-interim CEOs earlier in December, Wilson said the CEO succession plan was a "total failure of board oversight." "Shareholders have no faith that this board can select and support the next CEO without input from a board with stronger product experience," Wilson said in a public statement. On December 29, he confirmed that he has nominated three independent director candidates to the company's board, effectively launching a proxy fight at the athleisure brand. His nominations include former On Running co-CEO Marc Maurer, former ESPN chief marketing officer Laura Gentile, and former Activision CEO Eric Hirshberg. Lululemon responded later that day that it would evaluate Wilson's nominees. It also said that he initially withheld these names from the board. "We are encouraged by the strength we are seeing internationally and the work underway in the US, but we recognize that further opportunities exist to realize greater value across the company," it said. Years after he stepped down, he's still stirring controversy. Taehoon Kim/Bloomberg via Getty Images During a November leadership forum in Calgary hosted by Axis Connects, Wilson spoke to a crowd and proposed that women in Canada were not having enough children. The Guardian reported that the event was cut short 15 minutes early due to Wilson's comments. "There were audible gasps in the room, and everyone was clearly uncomfortable," an attendee told The Guardian. "It was a mix of disengaging, walking out and also just complete shock of what was being said on stage." The Guardian also reported that Wilson said that men were finding wives in Thailand because women were waiting too long to have children. Read the original article on Business Insider
